html:
In 218 BCE the Carthaginian general Hannibal marched an army from Spain over the Pyrenees, across southern Gaul and over the Alps into Italy, taking the Second Punic War to Rome's own soil.

Carthage, a Phoenician city in today's Tunisia, had lost Sicily to Rome in the First Punic War and built a new base in Spain. Rome held the sea, so Hannibal chose the long land route. He set out with tens of thousands of soldiers, cavalry and some 37 war elephants.

The crossing came in autumn, with snow on the passes, landslides and attacks by mountain tribes. He lost a large part of his army, and nearly all the elephants died soon after. Which pass he used is still argued.

In Italy he won crushing victories at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and, in 216 BCE, Cannae. But he never took Rome, and after fifteen years he was called home and beaten at Zama by Scipio in 202 BCE. Rome went on to destroy Carthage in 146 BCE.
sum: In 218 BCE the Carthaginian general Hannibal marched an army from Spain over the Pyrenees, across southern Gaul and over the Alps into Italy, taking the Second Punic War to Rome's own soil.
